video.title: EXACTLY How I Made $1M/Day Last Month (And What Went Wrong)

summary: David, founder and CEO of Filterbuy, explains how his US air filter manufacturing business reached more than $31 million in July as heat and wildfire smoke drove unexpected demand. The surge exposed weak inventory counts, order routing problems and a management gap after a regional leader resigned. He describes the operational changes that helped Filterbuy keep delivering and sustain sales momentum. His main lesson is to build and understand reliable operating systems before growth outstrips the ability to serve customers.

tactics.name: Choose a product suited to direct-to-consumer manufacturing
steps: Look for a product you can manufacture competitively in your home market.
Consider how product size and shipping costs affect the feasibility of importing it.
Use direct sales to the end customer to remove intermediaries.

quote.text: I wanted to own a product that I could manufacture competitively in the US and sell direct to consumer in the US.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Use daily operational dashboards and intervene early
steps: Build dashboards that show the health of each part of the operation.
Check them every morning and identify overloaded locations, stock problems and risks to delivery promises.
Shift eligible orders to centers that can still meet promised dates.
Add a delivery buffer when a center risks missing its promise.

quote.text: I was waking up at 5:30 in the morning. I was looking at the dashboards that we had built letting me know what's happening in any part of the business.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Rebalance production and inventory across locations
steps: Identify which centers are exceeding their production capacity and which have spare capacity.
Make additional product at centers with room to produce it.
Ship that product to the overloaded region.
Fix order routing so orders can move to locations with more capacity.

quote.text: We had a few centers, particularly in the Northeast, that got absolutely slammed. And when that happened, they were selling more than their production capabilities.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Treat inventory counts as an operating process
steps: Check that people follow the inventory-counting process consistently.
Investigate discrepancies quickly instead of treating them as a software-only problem.
Correct the counts and combine that work with routing and replenishment changes.

quote.text: Ultimately, the root cause here was a breakdown in our inventory system. Not from a software perspective, but from like the system of the people that are responsible for taking part in each of it.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Learn critical jobs and create a daily promise dashboard
steps: Write down every job in the business.
Mark the jobs you personally could not cover if the employee quit tomorrow.
Learn those jobs well enough to act as a fail-safe.
Build one dashboard around the key customer promise and check it every morning.

quote.text: Number one, write down every job in your business and mark the ones you personally could not do tomorrow if that person quit overnight.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Check delivery capacity before increasing demand
steps: Before spending more on ads or accepting more customers, assess whether the team can serve the orders already sold.
Fix service capacity and delivery reliability before pursuing more growth.

quote.text: Before you spend more on ads or take on more customers, be straight with yourself about whether you can service what you've already sold.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Visit newer locations to reinforce culture
steps: Identify newer locations, teams and hires where culture and process knowledge may be less established.
Spend time there in person, observe the work and discuss why the processes matter.

quote.text: If you've got a location, a team, or a hire that's newer than the rest, go spend time there in person
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: More sales can create operational problems if the business cannot deliver what it promised.

quote.text: If you don't do that delivery, your sales are ultimately going to go to zero because people are going to stop buying from you.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Keeping very little inventory leaves little margin for forecasting or counting errors.

quote.text: We keep less than two weeks of finished goods inventory across nine locations, and depending on how you look at it, that's either brilliant or insane.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: A robust software system can still fail when people do not follow the operating process.

quote.text: When you get pressure on a system like ours, you start to see weaknesses and weaknesses of maybe certain people were not following the process in the way that that process should be followed.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: A key employee can resign without notice, so the business should not depend on one person being the only fail-safe.

quote.text: Somebody will quit overnight. Mine did in the middle of the best month we'd ever had.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Delegating before learning how the work and systems function can prevent a founder from building a robust, scalable business.

quote.text: people are using that as an excuse to hire somebody to basically do all the work for them and if that's your mentality and that's your mindset, you're never going to build a robust business that is scalable.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Culture can weaken as a company adds locations if leaders do not spend time aligning people on the work and its purpose.

quote.text: the reality is that it's harder and harder to export that culture the larger that you get and the bigger that you get.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Choose a business where the product and market give you a structural advantage, such as manufacturing locally when shipping makes imports less practical.

quote.text: the person with the cost advantage ultimately is going to win.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Growth only helps when the business can keep the promises it makes to customers.

quote.text: sales is only one side of the equation. You have to also be able to deliver on whatever promise you're making to a customer.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Unexpected demand can reveal weaknesses in staffing, inventory, routing and management processes.

quote.text: when you get into stretch moments, a lot of times your first instinct is going to be to retreat.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Use operational metrics to spot problems early, then make specific changes such as rerouting orders or buffering delivery promises.

quote.text: we have operational dashboards that basically give us the health of every aspect of our business.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: When a serious operational failure happens, look for root causes and process gaps rather than assuming the software is at fault.

quote.text: Ultimately, the root cause here was a breakdown in our inventory system. Not from a software perspective
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: A founder can delegate more effectively after learning the work, documenting processes and building systems that can be handed to a capable steward.

quote.text: your job to build the systems, build the frameworks, get to escape velocity in those systems and frameworks, then that's when you earn the right to pass it off
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Newer teams and locations need direct attention because dashboards cannot show whether culture and process understanding are taking hold.

quote.text: that's where your culture is thinest, that's where it'll break, and you can't see it coming on any dashboard.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Treat business momentum as something to protect, while still fixing the operational issues that could undermine it.

quote.text: when you have momentum in business or you have momentum in life, that's when you want to double down, triple down.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Build inventory, routing and delivery systems by testing them under pressure, then making them more robust.

quote.text: the only way you're going to build those systems is by ultimately testing them, seeing where they're weak, and making them more robust
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Use the CEO role to support employees, understand root problems and remove blockers instead of simply taking over the work.

quote.text: Showing up as a CEO doesn't mean taking over.
quote.speaker: David Heacock

evidence_quality.rationale: David is a first-hand operator describing his own company, its operating processes and a specific demand surge. He gives many concrete figures, but they are self-reported and the transcript does not independently verify them.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: No sponsor or paid offer is disclosed. David mentions his own podcast and closes by directing viewers to another of his videos on building boring software.

extraction.review_notes: The extraction is thorough and the figures are accurate: revenue, volumes, locations, inventory weeks and the 99.5% on-time target all match the transcript. The main problem is an invented surname ("Heacock") for the speaker, who is identified only as David; it should be replaced in the speaker, summary, claimant and quote-speaker fields. One warning quote was not verbatim. The automation and UK scores, the B evidence rating and the idea coverage (the Filterbuy primary idea plus the passing mention of office-supply dropshipping) are reasonable.
